title: Lower UTI / Cystitis
subtitle: Dysuria, frequency, urgency — most common in women
content:
[DIAGNOSIS]
- Dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain
- Cloudy / malodorous urine
- Urine dipstick: positive for leukocytes + nitrites
- Uncomplicated — no fever, no flank pain

[INVESTIGATIONS]
- Urine analysis (routine urine): WBCs (pus cells), RBCs, bacteria — pyuria supports UTI
- Urine dipstick: leukocyte esterase and nitrite — quick bedside screen; negative nitrite does NOT exclude UTI
- Urine culture + sensitivity (MSU): for recurrent, complicated, pregnancy, pyelonephritis, treatment failure
- Renal function (Urea, Creatinine): guides antibiotic choice and dose adjustment
- CBC / CRP: if systemic infection or fever suspected
- Blood cultures: if high fever, rigors, or sepsis suspected
- Imaging (US KUB / CT): only if suspected obstruction, stone, abscess, recurrent complicated UTI, or no fever response at 48–72h

[TREATMENT]
- 1st line: Nitrofurantoin 100mg twice daily × 5 days
- OR Fosfomycin 3g single dose — convenient option
- Alternative (culture-guided): TMP-SMX if local resistance < 20%, or oral beta-lactam
- Fluoroquinolones are NOT first-line for uncomplicated UTI — reserve for complicated cases after culture
- Phenazopyridine: symptom relief only, ≤ 2–3 days
- Complicated / systemic: Ciprofloxacin or Ceftriaxone — usually 10–14 days
- Pregnancy: Nitrofurantoin (avoid near term ≥ 37 weeks and G6PD deficiency), Fosfomycin, or beta-lactam per culture

[WARNING]
Pyelonephritis in pregnancy → URGENT hospital admission + IV antibiotics. No clinical improvement in 48–72h → re-culture, re-examine, re-image — do not simply switch antibiotics. Nitrofurantoin and Fosfomycin have poor renal-tissue penetration — not for pyelonephritis.

title: Upper UTI / Pyelonephritis
subtitle: Fever, flank pain, nausea — infection ascending to kidney
content:
[DIAGNOSIS]
- Fever > 38.5°C, rigors, flank pain (CVA tenderness)
- Nausea, vomiting, malaise
- Blood cultures if sepsis suspected

[INVESTIGATIONS]
- Culture: Urine MC&S + blood cultures (if febrile/septic) before antibiotics
- Lab: CBC, CRP, renal function, electrolytes — assess severity and guide therapy
- Imaging: Renal ultrasound — exclude obstruction, renal abscess, calculi
- Monitor: Temperature, CVA tenderness, response to antibiotics at 48h; repeat if refractory

[TREATMENT]
- Mild-Moderate: Oral antibiotics 10–14 days
- Severe / Sepsis: IV antibiotics + admit
- Oral (mild): Ciprofloxacin 500mg BID × 7-14 days
- IV (severe): Ceftriaxone 1g OD IV

[WARNING]
Recurrent pyelonephritis: Investigate for structural abnormality (US renal, CT KUB) — rule out stones, obstruction, reflux.

title: Renal Colic / Urolithiasis
subtitle: Severe colicky flank pain radiating to groin — kidney stones
content:
[DIAGNOSIS]
- Severe colicky pain — comes in waves, intermits
- Radiates from flank to groin (loin to groin)
- Nausea, vomiting, hematuria

[INVESTIGATIONS]
- Imaging: CT KUB (non-contrast) — stone size, location, obstruction
- Lab: CBC, CRP, renal function, electrolytes, serum urate/calcium; urine dipstick (haematuria)
- Culture: Urine MC&S if infection suspected (obstructing infected stone = emergency)
- Monitor: Pain score, urine output, stone passage; renal function if obstruction

[TREATMENT]
- IV fluids if vomiting / dehydrated
- Strong analgesic — Ketorolac IM or Nalbuphine
- Antispasmodic — Drotaverine or Hyoscine
- Stone passage: Tamsulosin (medical expulsive therapy)

[WARNING]
Infected obstructing stone is a urological emergency — decompress with stent or percutaneous nephrostomy before antibiotics can work.

title: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia
subtitle: Elderly male — nocturia, weak stream, urgency, retention
content:
[DIAGNOSIS]
- IPSS score ≥ 8
- Urinary frequency, nocturia, weak stream, hesitancy
- Digital rectal exam: smooth, enlarged, non-tender prostate

[INVESTIGATIONS]
- Lab: PSA level (with age reference), renal function; urinalysis to exclude UTI
- Imaging: Renal USS + post-void residual volume (PVR) — assess obstruction
- Special test: Uroflowmetry, IPSS symptom score
- Monitor: IPSS score, PVR, PSA trend, response to medical therapy

[TREATMENT]
- Alpha-blocker: Tamsulosin 0.4mg — fast onset, first-line
- 5-ARI: Finasteride — shrinks prostate, takes 3–6 months
- Combo: Dutasteride + Tamsulosin — for large prostates

[WARNING]
Alpha-blockers can cause first-dose hypotension — take at bedtime. Avoid in patients on PDE5 inhibitors.

title: Overactive Bladder
subtitle: Urgency, frequency, nocturia, urge incontinence
content:
[DIAGNOSIS]
- Urgency — sudden compelling desire to void
- Frequency — > 8 times per 24 hours
- Nocturia — waking ≥ 2 times to void
- Diagnosis of exclusion — rule out UTI, diabetes, BPH

[INVESTIGATIONS]
- Lab: Urinalysis + MSU culture; FBS/HbA1c, renal function, electrolytes
- Special test: Bladder diary (frequency/volume), post-void residual, uroflowmetry
- Monitor: Symptom score (urgency, frequency, nocturia), response to anticholinergic
- Screen: BPH (PSA/DRE in men), diabetes, UTI as underlying causes

[TREATMENT]
- Step 1: Bladder training + fluid management
- Step 2: Anticholinergic (Oxybutynin / Tolterodine)
- Step 3: Switch to Solifenacin (better tolerated)
- Step 4: Beta-3 agonist (Mirabegron) or Botulinum toxin

[WARNING]
Oxybutynin causes significant dry mouth, constipation, and cognitive side effects in elderly — prefer Tolterodine or Solifenacin.

title: Sexually Transmitted Infections
subtitle: Urethritis, discharge, genital lesions — sexual health
content:
[DIAGNOSIS]
- Gonorrhea: Purulent discharge, dysuria
- Chlamydia: Mucoid discharge, often asymptomatic
- Herpes (HSV): Vesicles → ulcers, painful
- Syphilis: Painless chancre → rash

[INVESTIGATIONS]
- Culture: NAAT (nucleic acid amplification) for gonorrhoea/chlamydia from first-void urine/swabs
- Lab: HIV serology, RPR/VDRL (syphilis), HBsAg, hepatitis C, type-specific HSV serology
- Special test: Test of cure at 2 weeks; repeat screen at 3 months
- Monitor: Treatment completion, partner notification, symptom resolution

[TREATMENT]
- Treat empirically — don't wait for culture results
- Always treat sexual partners
- Screen for HIV and other STIs

title: Erectile Dysfunction
subtitle: Inability to achieve/maintain erection — assess cardiovascular risk
content:
[DIAGNOSIS]
- Check cardiovascular risk factors first
- Review medications (beta-blockers, SSRIs, antiandrogens)
- Hormonal: check testosterone, prolactin, TSH

[INVESTIGATIONS]
- Lab: Total testosterone (morning), prolactin, TSH, FSH/LH, fasting lipids, FBS, HbA1c
- ECG: Cardio risk assessment — coronary disease screen (stress test if risk factors)
- Special test: Glucose tolerance; penile duplex/ultrasound if vascular or anatomical cause
- Monitor: BP, lipid profile, cardiovascular risk, response to PDE5 inhibitors

[TREATMENT]
- Sildenafil: 50–100mg, 30–60 min before, with food
- Tadalafil: 10–20mg PRN or 5mg daily
- Start with lowest effective dose

[WARNING]
Absolute contraindication: PDE5 inhibitors + nitrates (GTN) = severe hypotension — potentially fatal.

title: Edema / Diuretic Therapy
subtitle: Peripheral edema, heart failure, liver disease, nephrotic syndrome
content:
[DIAGNOSIS]
- Cardiac: Heart failure — pitting, bilateral, ankles
- Hepatic: Liver cirrhosis — ascites + pedal edema
- Renal: Nephrotic syndrome — periorbital + generalized
- Drugs: CCBs, NSAIDs, steroids

[INVESTIGATIONS]
- Lab: Renal function, electrolytes, LFTs, albumin, urinalysis (proteinuria) — delineate cause
- Imaging: Echocardiogram (cardiac), liver ultrasound (cirrhosis/ascites)
- Special test: 24h urine protein if nephrotic syndrome; JVP assessment for cardiac cause
- Monitor: Daily weight, fluid balance, electrolytes (Na+/K+), renal function on diuretics

[TREATMENT]
- Mild edema: Thiazides (HCTZ) or K-sparing (Spironolactone)
- Moderate: Loop diuretics (Furosemide 20–40mg)
- Severe: High-dose loop ± thiazide combination

[WARNING]
Spironolactone + ACE inhibitors → hyperkalemia risk. Furosemide + Digoxin → hypokalemia → toxicity.
